analysis.one_liner: Requires companies and federal agencies to tell people when their personal data is breached.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required any federal agency or business that collects sensitive personal information — Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, biometric data — to notify affected people quickly after a breach, and to alert the Secret Service and state attorneys general when breaches were large. It let the Justice Department and state attorneys general sue companies that failed to notify, with fines up to $1 million per violation. It also would have replaced the patchwork of state breach-notification laws with a single national standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose records are exposed in a data breach. Today, whether you learn your Social Security number or card number was stolen depends largely on which state you live in; this bill would have set a nationwide duty to tell you without unreasonable delay, given you the breach details and credit bureau contact information, and made it easier to place a fraud alert on your credit file after a compromise notice.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers whose personal data is breached

how_it_helps.text: Requires federal agencies and businesses in interstate commerce to notify any U.S. resident whose sensitive personal information was, or is believed to have been, accessed in a breach, without unreasonable delay, with the burden on the company of proving it complied.

Notices must describe what data was taken, provide a toll-free number, and include credit reporting agency contact information; breaches affecting more than 5,000 people in a state also require media notice.
Amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act so a consumer who receives a compromise notice can place a fraud alert on their credit file with that notice alone, rather than needing an identity theft report.

Gives the Justice Department and state attorneys general power to sue companies that fail to notify, with civil penalties up to $1,000 per day per affected person, capped at $1 million per violation, and requires notice of large breaches to the Secret Service, FBI, Postal Inspection Service, and state attorneys general.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that hold customer data — retailers, banks, data handlers — bear the cost of notification, the risk of federal and state lawsuits, and penalties up to $1 million per violation. Those costs would be passed partly to consumers in prices. Federal agencies face the same notice duties, and Congress would have to fund Secret Service investigations and risk-assessment reviews.

drawbacks.text: The bill would supersede all state breach-notification laws for interstate businesses, replacing state standards — some of them tougher, with longer track records — with a single federal floor.
It creates no private right of action: an individual whose data was breached could not sue; only the Attorney General and state attorneys general could enforce the law.

It contains broad exits from the notice duty: companies can skip individual notice if a self-run risk assessment finds no significant risk of harm (subject to Secret Service review within 10 business days), encrypted data carries a presumption of no risk, and entities with card-blocking fraud-prevention programs are exempt in some card-only breaches.

Penalties are capped at $1 million per violation unless conduct was willful or intentional, and the same law enforcement agency (the Secret Service) that investigates breaches also reviews exemption claims, with its risk-assessment reports kept confidential from the public.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A national notice requirement would be a real gain for breach victims, who today get notice or not depending on state law. But the bill as written was a modest version of that gain: it preempted potentially stronger state laws, barred individual lawsuits, capped penalties at $1 million, and let companies route around notice through self-assessed risk reviews. An honest supporter would call it a floor, not a ceiling — and note that preemption makes the floor the ceiling too.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced late in the session, sent to four committees, referred to one subcommittee, and never moved again before the Congress ended in early January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the Data Breach Notification Act on September 28, 2010, less than three months before the 111th Congress ended.
The same day, it was referred to four committees — Energy and Commerce, Oversight and Government Reform, Financial Services, and Judiciary — meaning any one of them could have held it.
On December 20, 2010, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law; no hearings, markups, or votes followed.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and it received no further action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses holding consumer data are better off because the bill died: they face no national notification mandate, no federal penalty exposure, and no state-AG enforcement under it. The existing patchwork of state laws stays in place unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assigned it to four committees; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the remaining months of the session.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no member cosponsored the bill, so the record shows no partisan pattern either way.

industries.industry: Businesses that hold consumer data (retailers, banks, data handlers)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a nationwide duty to tell customers about breaches, exposed them to Justice Department and state-AG lawsuits, and set penalties up to $1 million per violation. Encryption safe harbors and self-run risk assessments softened the burden, but the core requirement is a direct cost to them and a direct protection for consumers.

Companies notifying more than 5,000 people must alert the nationwide credit bureaus, and consumers could place fraud alerts with a compromise notice alone — extra processing work, and free fraud alerts undercut sales of paid credit-monitoring products. The bureaus' interest in this bill ran against the consumers it served.
The bill creates a presumption of no notification duty for encrypted data, giving every data-holding business a reason to buy encryption and key-management tools.
